data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief reports results from the PISA 2012 assessment of creative problem solving, administered on computer to about 85,000 15-year-old students across 44 countries and economies. Problem-solving competence is defined as engaging in cognitive processing to understand and resolve problem situations where the solution method is not immediately obvious, including willingness to engage and regulate problem-solving processes. The brief compares mean problem-solving performance across countries/economies and also reports “stronger-than-expected” versus “weaker-than-expected” performance, where expected performance is estimated from a regression model conditional on students’ mathematics, reading, and science scores. It finds that Singapore and Korea rank highest, with Japan also performing strongly, and that many students lack basic problem-solving skills (e.g., only 31% in OECD countries can troubleshoot an unfamiliar malfunctioning device at Level 4). The document is descriptive and does not provide an ML modeling pipeline or performance metrics for predictive algorithms, so implications are framed as policy-relevant patterns rather than causal effects.
